title: HKMA self-assessment deadline lands today, STR backlog still open
summary: Today is the HKMA's annual AML/CFT self-assessment deadline. Hong Kong AIs with open Q4 2025 STR thematic findings face a double obligation. Plus: Australia's rate rise, and what Sibos 2026 signals for compliance infrastructure.
script:
JORDAN: Today is the thirtieth of September, which means Hong Kong authorised institutions had until close of business to file their annual AML and CFT self-assessment return under paragraph eleven of the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline. Alex, I want to start there, but not with the filing itself. I want to start with the institutions that are filing today while carrying open findings from the Q4 2025 STR thematic review.

ALEX: Right, and that is the combination that should concern people. The HKMA issued deficiency letters to roughly twenty-five percent of the authorised institution population earlier this year following that thematic review of STR narrative quality. Those findings are still open. Those institutions are now also submitting their annual self-assessment. The question I keep coming back to is: what does the examiner do with a self-assessment that covers STR governance when they already have an open deficiency letter in the file?

JORDAN: My read is they cross-reference immediately. The self-assessment asks you to certify the adequacy of your STR filing processes, your escalation chain, your training. If your narrative quality was found deficient in Q4, and you are now checking the box on STR governance in the self-assessment, that is a direct test of whether your remediation is credible or cosmetic.

ALEX: I think that is right, but I would push back slightly on the framing. The self-assessment under paragraph eleven is a structured return covering customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, STR filing, training, governance, and independent audit. It is not a deficiency-closure document. The HKMA will treat those as two separate tracks.

JORDAN: In theory, yes. In practice, the examiner reviewing your self-assessment will know you have an open letter. They work in the same supervisory division. Treating those as cleanly separate tracks is optimistic, and I think it is exactly the kind of optimism that gets MLROs into trouble at their next inspection.

ALEX: Fair. So the action here is obvious but needs stating clearly. If you are the MLRO at an HKMA-supervised authorised institution with an open Q4 2025 thematic finding, your self-assessment submission today is not the end of the obligation cycle. It is a checkpoint. You need a written remediation timeline that you can produce immediately if the HKMA asks. Not a plan you are still drafting, an actual document signed by a senior executive.

JORDAN: And if your institution received a deficiency letter and has not yet formally closed it with the HKMA, that is a conversation you need to have with your head of financial crime before the end of this week. Do not let that sit over a quarterly boundary.

ALEX: Moving on to Australia, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate target by twenty-five basis points yesterday to four point six percent. Now, this is not typically what we cover. But there is a genuine read-across for AML compliance that I think practitioners sometimes miss.

JORDAN: I agree it matters, and I will say why in a moment, but I want to name the reason it matters because I think you and I might frame it differently. My read is that rate rises change customer behaviour in ways that produce new typologies. Mortgage stress, drawdown patterns on credit facilities, unusual liquidity movements as customers restructure. Those are transaction-monitoring triggers that your current calibration may not be tuned for.

ALEX: That is the operational read, yes. My read is slightly different. From a supervisory perspective, when the rate environment shifts materially, AUSTRAC expects regulated entities to demonstrate that their risk-based systems and controls remain calibrated to the current environment. The annual AML and CTF Program review under section 84 of the AML and CTF Act was due at the end of August. If your board approved a program review before the rate environment shifted again, you may have an argument that the approved program is already stale.

JORDAN: That is a strong point. And it connects to something I would push compliance officers to do this week: pull your transaction-monitoring threshold documentation and check when it was last calibrated and against what environment. If the answer is more than twelve months ago and against a materially different rate environment, that is a gap you want to surface proactively, not defend reactively.

ALEX: The read-across for AUSTRAC-regulated entities specifically is to treat this rate movement as a trigger for a targeted review of your threshold logic, even if your full annual program review is already signed off.

JORDAN: Exactly. It does not require a full program resubmission. It requires a documented rationale that says we considered the changed environment and here is our assessment.

ALEX: Shifting our focus, Sibos 2026 opened in Miami yesterday. The three themes the conference is organised around are payment network interoperability, digital asset integration, and artificial intelligence in financial services infrastructure. For our listeners in APAC, I would flag the interoperability piece specifically.

JORDAN: Here is where I will push back on the conference framing a little. Sibos themes are aspirational. The compliance reality is that interoperability across payment rails creates correspondent banking complexity, and correspondent banking complexity is exactly where AML programs have historically underperformed. The FATF Recommendation 13 obligations on correspondent banking do not get easier when you add more rails. They get harder.

ALEX: Agreed, and I think the digital asset integration theme compounds that. If you are a compliance officer at a bank that is being asked to connect to a digital asset settlement layer for cross-border payments, the question for your risk committee is not whether the technology works. The question is whether your counterparty due diligence and your ongoing monitoring can cover the new typologies that layer introduces.

JORDAN: So the action for practitioners watching Sibos announcements come through this week: before any business team brings a new payment rail or digital asset integration to you for sign-off, make sure your third-party risk assessment process explicitly covers AML and CTF control adequacy, not just operational and cyber risk. That gap is a common finding.

ALEX: On a related note, the Paris-based compliance tooling firm Marble closed a six point five million euro Series A to scale its open-source AML and CFT automation platform. We note it without extensive analysis because the news cycle is full of these raises, and the compliance infrastructure investment theme is well established. What I would say is that the open-source framing is worth watching. Regulators in Singapore and Hong Kong have been signalling interest in auditable, explainable automated systems. Open-source tooling has a natural alignment with that expectation.

JORDAN: Useful context. The key word for any MLRO evaluating new tooling remains explainability. If your transaction-monitoring vendor cannot give you a clear audit trail for why an alert was raised or suppressed, that is a problem regardless of how sophisticated the underlying model is.

ALEX: Before we close, one watch item for tomorrow. The Singapore MAS Notice 626 quarterly STR governance review was due in mid-July. If you are a Singapore-regulated institution and that review has not been formally documented and signed off, it is overdue and should be your priority before the quarter closes tonight.

JORDAN: If any of that felt uncomfortably close to your current to-do list, it was meant to. The full obligation register and source links are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. We will be back tomorrow.
